newsitem.title: MALDIVES: S.Asian leaders to tackle poverty with trade.
newsitem.headline: S.Asian leaders to tackle poverty with trade.

text.p: The leaders of seven South Asian nations, representing one fifth of the world's population, meet this week to lend impetus to a fledgling campaign to catch up with powerful trading blocs in Southeast Asia and Europe.
The heads of government of the seven-nation South Asian Association for Regional Cooperation (SAARC) gather on this tiny Indian Ocean island nation for a three-day summit starting on Monday.

The leaders of Bangladesh, Bhutan, India, Maldives, Nepal, Pakistan and Sri Lanka were to begin arriving on Sunday at a resort on one of the 1,190 small coral islands that make up the tropical archipelago in the Indian Ocean.
The focus of the summit will be squarely on economics and trade, in line with a shift in the 12-year-old bloc's priorities away from geopolitical rivalries and towards business.
"The acceleration of economic cooperation has emerged as the core concern," said Kamlesh Sharma, a senior Indian Foreign Ministry official.

The task is daunting. The World Bank estimates that more than 500 million of the region's 1.2 billion people live in absolute poverty, where even their basic human needs are not met. Two of every five of the world's poor live in South Asia.

"South Asia is fast emerging as the poorest, the most illiterate, the most malnourished, the least gender-sensitive -- indeed, the most deprived region in the world," the Islamabad-based Human Development Centre said in a recent report.
Annual per capita income in South Asia is $309 -- the lowest in the world and well below the $555 of sub-Saharan Africa and $825 in East Asia excluding China, the report said.

SAARC has increasingly concentrated its energies on promoting trade among its disparate members, which range from the tiny Himalayan kingdoms of Bhutan and Nepal to the world's largest democracy, India.
The region took the first steps towards forming a trade bloc in 1995 with the creation of the South Asian Preferential Trade Agreement (SAPTA), vowing to form a free-trade zone by 2005.

SAARC member countries have agreed to reduce tariffs on more than 1,700 items. But some 4,500 remain untouched, and commerce between the seven SAARC countries accounts for only three percent of their total trade.
The region trades far more with the 15 member states of the European Union, the Association of South East Asian Nations (ASEAN) and the North American Free Trade Agreement than between themselves.
The modest level of trade between India and Pakistan is a telling example of the gap between aspirations and reality.
Two-way trade between the neighbours totalled $115 million in the year to March 1996. India traded more than three times as much with Sri Lanka and nine times more with Bangladesh.

Mistrust between India and Pakistan has hampered SAARC's efforts to spur trade and spoiled some SAARC summits. South Asia is the only region where military spending as a share of economic output has gone up since 1987.
But the two longtime rivals have launched peace talks, and their prime ministers were set to meet on Monday in the Maldives.
India will press its partners to consider modelling SAARC on the European Union and adopting a single currency.
"The European Union concept might sound a bit far-fetched now, but by the turn of the century, it would be the crying need among SAARC nations," Indian Foreign Secretary Salman Haider said last week.
"The goal is the free flow of trade, capital, people and even to start a SAARC currency," Sharma said.

SAARC leaders are also expected to endorse an agreement reached by their foreign ministers at the weekend to relax visa requirements for 10 categories of travellers, including SAARC ministers and the heads of international sports organisations.
